text:
Alice M.: Heads up — we need a concrete design for mixed-capacity pools that lets us lower the global on-demand floor without risking 99th%-tile latency regressions. Sketch: per-tenant "burst tokens" + "interruption credits" + AZ-level min_on_demand. Thoughts?

Ben Y.: Sounds promising. Do you mean tokens allocated monthly based on commit or dynamic by recent usage? any target numbers?

Carla S.: FWIW region behaviour matters a lot. last month us-west1 had three big spot drains around 08:00 UTC, zone-level revocation correlated w/ scheduled maintenance. If we reduce floor too much we see correlated failures across tenants. Need AZ min + cross-AZ fallback.

Dan R.: Proposal idea: keep a tiny guaranteed on-demand floor per-AZ (min_on_demand_az = max(1, ceil(α * tenant_qps))). Allow tenants to burst above that using burst_tokens. Tokens are consumed when we replace interrupted spot instances with on-demand warm replacements. Tokens regen at some rate and can be topped up by committed capacity.

Alice M.: Yeah — tokens act as a short-lived credit to pay for the latency cost of immediate hot replacement. Also add interruption_credits that represent expected spot unreliability: if the score for an AZ goes bad we start saving tokens rather than burning them.

Carla S.: One operational gotcha — model artifact pulls + init = ~30-45s cold GPU start in many clusters (network and caching limits). If you immediately spin on-demand to replace, you need warm caches. tokens should encode both count and "warm-credit" (time to warm state).

Dan R.: Rough policy sketch (pseudo-config):

```
policy {
  min_on_demand_az = max(1, ceil(0.05 * tenant_qps))
  burst_tokens = { capacity: 12, regen_per_hour: 3 }
  warm_credit_seconds = 45
  interrupt_handling = "hot_replacement_if_tokens"
  eviction_priority = ["best_effort", "batch", "interactive"]
}
```

Ben Y.: Nice. Metrics to track: token_burn_rate, token_regen_rate, replacement_latency (time from spot interrupt -> on-demand ready), p99_latency_by_tenant, and cost_delta_by_tenant. We should simulate before rollout.

Eva L.: For simulation: take historical spot revocation traces per-AZ (last 90d), model warm-up distribution (we have bench data), run Monte Carlo for token pools of sizes 6/12/24 and regen rates 1/3/6/hr. Output: expected interruptions avoided, additional on-demand hours consumed, and p99 latency tail risk.

Carla S.: Also add a hard global cap: no tenant can borrow more than X% of total burst tokens in an AZ concurrently — prevents noisy neighbor bursting to DDoS on-demand capacity.

Dan R.: Agree. Also suggest a circuit-breaker: if AZ-level interruption_rate > threshold T, temporarily increase min_on_demand_az and pause token regen for new allocations. That protects critical tenants.

Alice M.: Good call. We should also consider network throttles when many GPUs fetch artifacts simultaneously. One mitigation: pre-warm by keeping a tiny warm pool of on-demand instances flagged as "artifact-cached" that are eligible for token-driven swap. They count against a different budget.

infra-bot: benchmark: model load median=28s, p95=44s, p99=72s (from warm-start-runner/2026-02-18).

Ben Y.: Action items: 1) Dan + Eva build Monte Carlo sim using 90d traces, produce table for token capacities/regens. 2) Carla + infra team check artifact caching + warm pool feasibility & estimated cost. 3) Alice to draft rollout plan: alpha tenants, observability (token burn dashboard + alerts).

Alice M.: I'll draft the rollout doc. Quick question for Dan — how hard is implementing token accounting in our scheduler? estimate dev effort?

Dan R.: Basic accounting + policy checks ~2 wks (eng-infra), additional 1-2 wks for AZ circuit-breaker and warm-pool prioritization. Need a small API surface for ops to top-up tokens for enterprise commits.

Eva L.: I'll start on the sim and post results here. Prefer a conservative alpha: tokens=12, regen=3/hr, warm_pool=2 per-AZ.

Alice M.: Perfect. Thanks all — keep replies short if you have objections. If none by EOD, I'll turn this into a doc and PR. :thumbsup:
